title: Module 1 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A larger sample always eliminates sampling error.
items.why: Larger samples reduce sampling error on average, but a sample is never the whole population, so some error always remains.

items.s: A statistic and a parameter are the same thing as long as the sample is random.
items.why: They are different quantities. A random sample makes the statistic a good estimate of the parameter, but they are rarely identical.

items.s: A correlational study can show that one variable causes another.
items.why: Without manipulation and random assignment, a third variable or reverse direction can explain the relationship.

items.s: Ordinal data tell you the order of cases but not how far apart they are.
items.why: That is the defining limit of the ordinal scale.

items.s: A score of 0 on an interval scale means the complete absence of the attribute.
items.why: An arbitrary zero is the mark of an interval scale. Only ratio scales have a true zero.

items.s: Whether a rating scale from 1 to 7 is treated as interval or ordinal
items.why: Researchers often treat summed rating scales as interval, but a single item is arguably ordinal. The decision is a judgment about what the numbers mean.

items.s: Descriptive statistics let you draw conclusions about a population.
items.why: Descriptive statistics summarize the data in hand. Inferential statistics generalize to a population.

items.s: Random sampling and random assignment are the same thing.
items.why: Random sampling is how you select participants and supports generalizing. Random assignment is how you place them in conditions and supports cause and effect.
